title: Solve it together: warmest day (with a cold snap)
idea: GUIDED via UEPCC. Apply MAX to temperatures that include negatives — why the start value matters.
problem: Daily temps are [-2, -5, -1, -8]. What was the warmest day?

exercises.prompt:
PROBLEM: temps [-2, -5, -1, -8]. Warmest day?

What is the OUTPUT?
exercises.explanation: 'Warmest' is the biggest value — max — even when all values are negative.

exercises.prompt: All the temperatures are below zero. Does max still apply?
options: Yes — the 'biggest' is the one closest to zero
No — max only works on positives
exercises.explanation: Max finds the biggest value whatever the signs. Among negatives, biggest means closest to zero.

exercises.prompt: Example by hand. Among [-2, -5, -1, -8], which is the warmest (biggest)?
exercises.explanation: -1 is closest to zero, so it is the biggest. That is your check value.

exercises.prompt: Plan. Where must the best-so-far start so negatives work?
exercises.explanation: Start at the first real value. Starting at 0 would wrongly win, since 0 is bigger than every temp here.

exercises.prompt: If best started at 0, the code would report 0 — a temperature that never happened.
exercises.explanation: No negative beats 0, so best would stay 0. That bug is why we start at temps[0].

exercises.prompt: Code it. Arrange the lines to find the warmest day.
exercises.explanation: Start best at temps[0], loop, replace when bigger, print the warmest.
temps[0] is the first real value — safe even when every value is negative.

exercises.prompt: Check. The code prints -1. Your hand example said -1. So...
exercises.explanation: Output matches the hand-found warmest, so the max solution is correct even with negatives.

exercises.prompt: New input: temps = [-10, -10, -3]. With the same code, what prints?
exercises.explanation: -3 is the biggest (warmest). Starting at the first value let the negatives compare correctly.

exercises.prompt: Testing on an all-negative list is a good way to prove your max code starts safely.
exercises.explanation: All-negative lists expose the 'started at 0' bug. Passing this test builds confidence.
